feedback: Confirm the efficient pair (e.g. 7 + 3) and point out that it is not the first two numbers written.
If the child selects the first two numbers by default, ask 'can you see two that make ten?' and rehearse the relevant bond.
Keep any timing light and supportive so it builds automaticity rather than anxiety.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent recall of bonds to 10 lets you spot the useful pair quickly; deliberately choosing a make-ten pair can make the addition quicker and less error-prone than always adding left-to-right.
learnerActions: Given a triple such as 5 + 7 + 3, choose which two numbers you would add first and say why.
Complete fill-in-the-blank totals for a set of triples, each containing a make-ten pair that is not the first two written.
Do a short, light timed set of spotting make-ten pairs to build quick recall of bonds to 10.
For each item, state the pair chosen and the leftover number before giving the total.
activities.title: Which pair makes it easiest? — fluency and strategy choice

feedback: If the child narrates adding the first two written numbers every time, highlight the ten pair and rehearse the scan-first habit — the skill, not the concept, is what's missing.
If the child insists numbers must be added in written order, demonstrate that reordering keeps the total the same (any two may be added first).
When a pair makes ten but the third number is lost or doubled, bring the third number in last and recount.
activities.intendedInsight: Explaining the chosen pair makes the scanning strategy explicit and surfaces whether the child is truly scanning or just adding in written order.
learnerActions: A tutor poses triples such as 5 + 7 + 3, 8 + 2 + 6 and 4 + 9 + 1.
For each, work out the total and say which two numbers you added first and why that choice helps.
Answer follow-ups: 'Is there a pair here that makes exactly ten?', 'Would you get the same total in a different order?', 'For 4 + 9 + 1, which pair makes ten and which number is left to add on?'
activities.title: Narrate the pair you chose

feedback: Point to the highlighted pair and the resulting 'ten and a bit' to anchor the method.
Note that this is an example to study: it shows the method but does not give feedback on the child's own attempts, so follow it with hands-on practice.
activities.intendedInsight: A clear model of the scan-pair-add sequence gives a reference point for the strategy before independent practice.
learnerActions: Study a worked triple, e.g. 5 + 7 + 3, with the 7 + 3 pair highlighted as it makes ten.
Follow the two steps: pair to ten (7 + 3 = 10), then add the third (5 + 10 = 15).
Describe in your own words how the pair was chosen before moving to practice items.
activities.title: Worked anchor: see the make-ten pair highlighted
